title: Is the Yonaguni Monument a Man-Made Ice Age Structure?
site_name: Ancient Origins Reconstructing the story of humanity's past
excerpt: Giant underwater steps off the island of Yonaguni in southern Japan are often described online as the ruins of a city built before the end of the last Ice Age. The geologist who made that case still has supporters, but most geologists who have studied the rock read it as natural sandstone shaped by the sea.

Fact Check verdict: Disputed. Masaaki Kimura argues from his own surveys that people carved it about 10,000 years ago, but geologists who have studied the site describe natural sandstone shaped along joints and layers, and no securely dated artifacts tie it to builders.

Yonaguni is a small island at the western end of Japan's Yaeyama chain, about 111 kilometers from the coast of Taiwan. In shallow water off its southern tip lies a block of rock with flat terraces, straight walls and what look like giant steps, a site divers call the Yonaguni Monument.

To many viewers, the shapes look too regular to be natural. A Japanese geologist has argued that it is a stepped pyramid carved by people when the sea was much lower, near the end of the last Ice Age, so does the evidence support the idea?

According to the published research, the answer is still argued, but the weight of geological work favors a natural origin.

What the formation is

A local diver first noticed the formations in 1986, National Geographic reported in 2007. Masaaki Kimura, a marine geologist at the University of the Ryukyus, began surveys with his university team in 1992, according to his own account.

In a 2004 paper for the Oceans'04 conference, Kimura placed the main formation about 100 meters off Cape Arakawa-bana. He described it as a rough rectangle about 270 meters long and 26 meters high, with its upper terrace only 5 meters below the surface.

He also described the rock. The formation, he wrote, is "a monolithic structure composed of layers of sandstone and mudstone." He granted that "It would be relatively simple for natural forces to separate the layers," which could then fracture and slip into flat terraces and straight walls.

The case for a man-made structure

Kimura's argument is that the shapes go beyond what nature can do. In the 2004 paper he lists flat terraces, a pool with vertical walls, a feature he calls a loop road, drainage channels, stairways and a retaining wall, along with the lack of fallen rubble at its foot.

He also reports rows of funnel-shaped holes that he reads as wedge marks. He wrote that "Tool marks in stone are the strongest evidence so far supporting a man-made explanation for the structure."

The paper also describes two stone tools collected nearby, a small tablet with two scratched marks and a cobble he reads as a carved animal. Kimura dates the work to about 10,000 years ago, citing radiocarbon and beryllium measurements on more than 40 samples, and argues that rising seas after the Ice Age drowned it.

In a 2007 National Geographic report, Toru Ouchi, a seismologist at Kobe University who had dived the site, said that "It's easy to tell that those relics were not caused by earthquakes."

Rock ledges on the Main Terrace that look like giant steps. Photo by Melkov, 2019, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0, resized.

What the evidence says

Robert Schoch, a professor of science and mathematics at Boston University, made dozens of dives at the site. On his website he concludes that "it is primarily a natural structure." He explains that "The rocks of the region break out neatly, both along horizontal and vertical planes, and naturally form the step-like appearance."

Schoch also told National Geographic that the holes Kimura reads as post holes were scoured by eddies, and that the lines of smaller holes were made by marine creatures along a seam in the rock. He added that the formations are "not as regular as many people claim, and the right angles and symmetry don't add up in many places."

A peer-reviewed 2020 study of Yonaguni's geology in the journal E-journal GEO, led by Takayuki Ogata of the University of the Ryukyus, reaches a similar view. Writing in Japanese, the authors note that the straight lines may look artificial, but that almost the same forms occur on land at Sanninu-dai, a coastal site to the northeast, translated here by Ancient Origins. They attribute both to weathering and erosion controlled by the layers and straight joints of the sandstone, and call this a common landform on the island's south coast.

They add that before sea levels rose about 10,000 years ago, the underwater site and Sanninu-dai were likely part of one rocky coast shaped by the same processes. Kimura, in his 2004 paper, instead describes Sanninu-dai as a similar construction on land.

Tools, dates and records

The most detailed recent survey comes from a Kyushu University team led by Hironobu Kan, which mapped the seafloor with sonar, an underwater robot and years of dives. In a 2024 conference summary, also in Japanese and translated here by Ancient Origins, the team reports that no archaeological artifacts or human traces have been detected on these flat-topped forms, which are made of layered sandstone and mudstone cut by many joints. They also saw erosion at work, with potholes still forming.

Kimura's stone tools were collected near the formation and dated by comparison with similar tools elsewhere, so they do not on their own show who shaped the rock or when. His age estimates have also moved. His 2004 paper gives about 10,000 years, while National Geographic reported in 2007 that he dated the ruins to at least 5,000 years.

National Geographic also reported that neither Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs nor Okinawa Prefecture recognized the site as an important cultural property.

The sea above the Yonaguni Monument. According to the photographer, the underwater formation lies to the right of the rocks breaking the surface, and layered rock shows in the cliff at left. Photo by Melkov, 2013, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0, resized.

The alternative view

The appeal of the man-made reading is easy to see. Flat surfaces, sharp edges and steps close to right angles are what people expect from masonry, and Kimura himself wrote that the formation "would seem to have been formed by nature at first glance." His own first impression, he told National Geographic, was the same until his first dive.

Schoch suggested to National Geographic that many photos frame the site in ways that make the lines look as regular as possible. He has also written that people living on the island may have admired the formation, and that small parts may have been "touched up" by them.

Where this leaves it

Kimura's case rests on his own surveys and readings, and he has some support. Against it stand geologists who have dived and mapped the site and describe natural sandstone, and a recent survey that found no archaeological remains.

Background is in the Yonaguni Monument atlas entry and in an earlier Ancient Origins look at whether Yonaguni is man-made or natural. Another case of shapes read as modern work is in the Abydos helicopter Fact Check.

How we checked this

Read for this check were Kimura's 2004 paper and 2003 abstract, the studies by Ogata's and Kan's teams, Schoch's own account and the 2007 National Geographic report. Japanese passages were translated by Ancient Origins and appear only as paraphrase.

Kimura's 1999 dating report could not be opened because the repository was offline, and a New Scientist article refused access. Earlier Ancient Origins coverage was not a source, and the labels are explained on the evidence standards page.

A diver above the flat area known to divers as the Main Terrace at the Yonaguni Monument, off the south coast of Yonaguni Island, Japan. Photo by Melkov, 2019, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/), cropped and resized

By Aris Manus

Claim by claim

  • Disputed: The Yonaguni underwater monument is a man-made Ice Age structure. Reason: Kimura argues it, while other geologists who studied the site describe natural sandstone.
  • Established: The formation lies in shallow water off the south coast of Yonaguni and was noticed by a local diver in 1986. Reason: Kimura locates it and National Geographic dates the find.
  • Established: The rock is layered sandstone and mudstone cut by joints. Reason: Kimura and the other geologists agree on the rock.
  • Established: Similar stepped forms occur on land at Sanninu-dai. Reason: a peer-reviewed 2020 study describes them.
  • Unverified: Tool marks and objects from the site prove human builders. Reason: only Kimura reports them as such.
  • Unverified: The formation was shaped about 10,000 years ago. Reason: Kimura's own estimates have varied, and his dating reports could not be opened.
